n: This lecture is devoted to pyrazole derivatives. The outline: pyrazole derivatives, namely phenazone, or antipyrine, propyphenazone, or amidopyrine, metamizole sodium, or analgin, and phenylbutazone, or butadione; their isolation and analysis. Key terms: a polar solvent and these four substances. The topic belongs to the section on the analysis of weakly basic and acidic substances in isolates.

The plan and outcome of the laboratory class. Plan: to study the toxicological significance and methods of analysis of pyrazole derivatives, as well as phenacetin, salicylic acid and acetylsalicylic acid. Expected outcome: to master qualitative reactions in a pure and in an unknown solution. The result is recorded in the lab notebook and confirmed by the teacher. Equipment: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual aids.

Let us clarify the names of the pyrazole derivatives. Phenazone is antipyrine; propyphenazone is amidopyrine, that is, pyramidone; metamizole sodium is analgin; phenylbutazone is butadione. Antipyrine: 1,5-dimethyl-2-phenylpyrazol-3-one, international name phenazone. Amidopyrine: 1-phenyl-2,3-dimethyl-4-dimethylamino-5-pyrazolone, international name aminophenazone. The international name of analgin is dipyrone, or metamizole, while butadione is 1,2-diphenyl-4-butylpyrazolidine-3,5-dione.

The role of pyrazole derivatives in isolation and re-extraction. They are extracted with acidified water or alcohol in acidic and alkaline media. Part of the antipyrine passes into the organic solvent layer under acidic conditions, and the main part under alkaline conditions. During purification by repeated extraction, that is, re-extraction, substances with weakly basic properties are lost: purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrine.

General characteristics of antipyrine. Antipyrine is used as an antipyretic and analgesic. It is a colourless crystalline powder, freely soluble in water, alcohol and chloroform. When applied locally it has a haemostatic effect and reduces capillary absorption.

Physicochemical data of antipyrine. Neutral in nature; CAS 60-80-0; melting point 111-113 °C; pKa 1.4. Solubility: in chloroform 1:1, in water 1:1, in ethanol 1:1.3, in ether 1:43. The half-life is 7-15 hours, and Vd is 0.56 L/kg.

Absorption and elimination of antipyrine. Antipyrine is rapidly absorbed from the digestive tract into the blood and reaches its maximum blood concentration within 1-2 hours. In the body 30-40 % is conjugated with glucuronic acid and excreted as the glucuronide. Part is hydroxylated to form 4-hydroxyantipyrine. 5 % is excreted unchanged in the urine.

t: Antipyrine: symptoms of poisoning and metabolites
n: Symptoms of antipyrine poisoning and its metabolites. Body temperature falls, there is nausea and vomiting, breathing becomes difficult and the heart rate slows. The person becomes drowsy, delirious and finally loses consciousness. Metabolites: 4-hydroxyantipyrine, 30-40 %; 3-hydroxymethylantipyrine, 10 %; n-hydroxyantipyrine; norantipyrine, 6 %. A further 5 % is excreted unchanged within 24 hours.

t: Antipyrine: general precipitating reagents and FeCl3
n: Reactions of antipyrine with general precipitating reagents and iron(III) chloride. With general, that is, alkaloid, reagents it forms a precipitate. With iron(III) chloride it gives blood-red ferripyrine. With Liebermann's reagent it gives an orange colour, and with Mandelin's reagent a green colour.

The ferripyrine reaction. Antipyrine forms blood-red ferripyrine with iron(III) chloride. In practice, 0.5 ml of 5 % FeCl3 is added to 1 ml of solution. If antipyrine is present, a red colour appears; if amidopyrine, a violet colour. Remember: the colour formed disappears under an excess of the reagent.

The nitroso reaction of antipyrine. With sodium nitrite in an acidic medium, antipyrine forms green nitrosoantipyrine. If there is a lot of antipyrine, a green precipitate may form. If α-naphthylamine is added to nitrosoantipyrine, a red pyrazolone dye is formed.

Formation of the pyrazolone dye. Antipyrine with sodium nitrite and HCl gives green nitrosoantipyrine. If α-naphthylamine is added to the nitrosoantipyrine formed, a red pyrazolone dye is produced. If there is a lot of antipyrine, a green precipitate may form. In other words, the reaction proceeds in two stages: first a green, then a red product.

t: Antipyrine and amidopyrine: practical work with nitrite
n: Practical determination of antipyrine and amidopyrine with nitrite. To 1 ml of the test solution, add a few drops of 10 % sulphuric acid and 2-3 drops of saturated sodium nitrite solution. If antipyrine is present, a blue-green colour appears; if amidopyrine, a violet colour. If both are present, the violet colour of amidopyrine appears first. With excess nitrite it fades, and a blue-green colour, that is, the colour of nitrosoantipyrine, develops.

TLC and spectral data of antipyrine. In thin-layer chromatography, TLC: silica gel G, 250 µm, mobile phase methanol and 25 % ammonia in the ratio 100:1.5; visualising reagent iron(III) chloride; Rf = 0.65, spot red. In the UV spectrum there are maxima at 230 nm in 0.1 N HCl and at 242 and 256 nm in alkaline solution. In the IR spectrum, in KBr: 1660, 770, 1318, 1305, 1590 and 1580 cm⁻¹; in the mass spectrum: 188, 96, 77, 56, 105, 189, 55 and 51 m/z.

Quantitative determination of antipyrine. Antipyrine forms a precipitate with picric acid. After the precipitate is separated, the excess picric acid is determined by titration. Antipyrine is also determined by UV spectrophotometry. GLC and HPLC methods are also indicated for quantitative determination.

General characteristics of amidopyrine. Amidopyrine, that is, pyramidone, is a colourless crystalline substance, freely soluble in water, chloroform and ethyl alcohol. In medicine it is used as an analgesic and anti-cold agent. With prolonged use, in some cases the function of the haematopoietic organs is impaired and skin rashes appear.

Physicochemical data of amidopyrine. Formula C13H17N3O; CAS 58-15-1; melting point 107-109 °C; pKa 5.0. Solubility: in chloroform 1:1, in ethanol 1:1.5, in water 1:18, in ether 1:13, in petrol 1:12. The half-life is 1.7-3.1 hours.

Toxicological significance and metabolism of amidopyrine. Its toxicological significance is similar to that of antipyrine. In the body amidopyrine can be converted into 4-aminoantipyrine, methylaminoantipyrine, and the red-coloured rubazonic and methylrubazonic acids. Therefore the urine of people who have taken a large dose is stained red. The oxyamidopyrine formed by oxidation is reddish in colour.

Metabolite percentages of amidopyrine. In metabolism, 4-methylaminoantipyrine accounts for 3-4 %, 4-formylaminoantipyrine for 20 %, 4-aminoantipyrine for 4-8 %, and 4-acetylaminoantipyrine for 20-48 %. About 1-3 % is excreted unchanged in the urine. Amidopyrine is oxidised and converted into reddish oxyamidopyrine.

Colour reactions of amidopyrine. It gives a precipitate with general precipitating reagents. Iron(III) chloride gives a rapidly fading violet colour. In an acidic medium with sodium nitrite, a violet colour that fades with excess reagent is formed. It reduces silver from silver nitrate solution: a pink colour and a black precipitate appear.

The reaction of amidopyrine with silver nitrate. Amidopyrine reduces silver from silver nitrate solution, producing a pink colour and a black precipitate. In practice, 3-5 drops of 1 % AgNO3 are added to 1 ml of solution and heated on a water bath for 3-5 minutes; a violet colour indicates amidopyrine. In TLC, in the system chloroform and acetone, 9:1, with Dragendorff's reagent it gives a brown spot, Rf = 0.15; 0.17.

Amidopyrine: the chromotropic acid reaction and TLC. If sulphuric acid and then chromotropic acid are added to amidopyrine, a pink colour appears. The reason is that concentrated H2SO4 cleaves amidopyrine to form formaldehyde, which gives a pink colour with chromotropic acid. In TLC, in chloroform and acetone, 9:1, with Dragendorff's reagent a brown spot is formed, Rf = 0.15; 0.17.

t: Case problem: pink colour with chromotropic acid
n: A case problem. A person who drank a large amount of a bitter-tasting medicine developed, after 4-5 hours, a fall in temperature, vomiting and difficulty breathing, and the urine was red-brown. In the preliminary analysis, when concentrated H2SO4 and chromotropic acid were added to the chloroform isolate, a pink colour appeared. Discussion: in concentrated H2SO4 amidopyrine is cleaved to formaldehyde and gives a pink colour with chromotropic acid.

Additional methods and quantification of amidopyrine. With Liebermann's reagent it gives a blue colour. Amidopyrine can also be identified by its UV and IR spectra. Its amount is determined by an extraction-photometric method based on the complex with bromophenol blue.

t: Case problem: red urine and methaemoglobinaemia
n: Another case problem. The urine sample is red; the kidneys show signs of nephritis, and the blood test showed methaemoglobinaemia. For discussion: when amidopyrine is taken in a large dose, the urine is stained red because of rubazonic and methylrubazonic acids. Phenacetin, in turn, in a large dose can cause methaemoglobinaemia, anaemia and nephritis.

General characteristics of analgin. The use and toxicological significance of analgin are similar to those of antipyrine. In medicine it is an analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic agent. It is an odourless, slightly bitter, whitish-yellowish needle-like crystalline powder. If used incorrectly, it leads to poisoning.

Physicochemical data of analgin. International name dipyrone, or metamizole; weakly basic in nature; melting point 172 °C. Solubility: in ethanol 1:30, in water 1:1.5; practically insoluble in ether, petrol, acetone and chloroform. The half-life is 2-4 hours, and Vd is 1.2 L/kg.

Qualitative reactions of analgin. With a solution of benzoquinone in acetic acid it gives a cherry-red colour. With iron(III) chloride it gives a rapidly fading violet product. With Nessler's reagent it forms a red-yellow precipitate.

The benzoquinone reaction of analgin. A solution of benzoquinone in acetic acid forms a cherry-red product with analgin. The amount of analgin is determined from this colour by the photoelectrocolorimetric method. In the UV spectrum, a solution in 0.1 N HCl has an absorption maximum at 258 nm.

t: Analgin: reactions in the practical class
n: Analgin: reactions in the practical class. Analgin forms a precipitate with alkaloid precipitating reagents. With KIO3 in the presence of HCl it gives a red colour; with excess reagent a dark red colour and a brown precipitate form. If dilute HCl and chloramine B are added to the aqueous solution, a yellow colour appears. In the UV spectrum, a solution in 0.1 N HCl has an absorption maximum at 258 nm.

TLC and quantitative determination of analgin. In TLC, acetone and chloroform in the ratio 1:9 are used; when sprayed with Dragendorff's reagent a brown spot forms, which is compared with the spot of the standard substance. In the qualification material, in the system methanol and 25 % ammonia, 100:1.5, Rf = 0.84, brown spot. The amount is determined by the photoelectrocolorimetric method from the colour obtained with benzoquinone.

Metabolism of analgin. In the body analgin is broken down into 4-methylaminoantipyrine, 3.5 %, 4-aminoantipyrine, 9.2 %, 4-formylaminoantipyrine, 16 %, and 4-acetylaminoantipyrine, 15-31 %. Of it, 70 % is excreted unchanged in the urine. A small amount of unchanged substance is excreted in the urine over 3 days.

Properties of butadione, that is, phenylbutazone. Butadione is a white or slightly yellowish powder; insoluble in water, slowly soluble in alcohol. It dissolves readily in ether, acetone, chloroform and alkalis; it melts at 104-107 °C. In medicine it is used as an analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic agent, in gout and rheumatoid polyarthritis.

Metabolism and identification of butadione. In metabolism hydrazobenzene is formed; about 10-15 % is excreted unchanged in the urine. It gives a precipitate with alkaloid reagents and forms a coloured product with iron(III) chloride. With copper(II) sulphate it gives a grey precipitate, which then turns pale blue. With NaNO2 and H2SO4 a dark orange and then dark red azo dye, that is, azobenzene, is formed.

Separating three substances by TLC. Alcoholic solutions of antipyrine, amidopyrine and analgin are spotted at 1 cm intervals on a KSK plate. After the system acetone and chloroform, 1:9, has risen 10 cm, the plate is dried and sprayed with FeCl3. Antipyrine forms a red spot, amidopyrine a violet one, analgin a blue one; Rf = 0.15-0.17.

t: TLC: procedure for identifying pyrazole derivatives
n: Procedure for identifying pyrazole derivatives by TLC. The start line is drawn on a plate containing KSK; alcoholic solutions of antipyrine, amidopyrine and analgin are spotted at 1 cm intervals. The chamber is saturated with acetone and chloroform, 1:9; after the system has risen 10 cm the plate is dried and sprayed with FeCl3. Rf is calculated by the formula Rf = a / b: a is the distance from the start line to the centre of the spot, and b is the distance from the start line to the finish line.

Let us compare all three substances. Antipyrine: red with FeCl3, that is, ferripyrine; green nitrosoantipyrine with NaNO2. Amidopyrine: rapidly fading violet with FeCl3; pink with chromotropic acid. Analgin: cherry-red with benzoquinone; red-yellow precipitate with Nessler's reagent.

Questions to test your knowledge. First: why does phenacetin pass into the organic solvent layer in an acidic medium, and how do you explain its toxicological significance? Second: write the equations for the reactions of phenacetin forming an azo dye, with chromic anhydride, and forming nitrosophenacetin; can it be identified by TLC? Third: which substances are pyrazole derivatives, and how do you explain their toxicological and narcological significance?

Let us summarise. Pyrazole derivatives: antipyrine, amidopyrine, analgin and butadione; isolates are obtained under acidic and alkaline conditions. Antipyrine gives ferripyrine with FeCl3 and nitrosoantipyrine with NaNO2; amidopyrine is identified with chromotropic acid via formaldehyde; analgin is identified with benzoquinone. In TLC, in acetone and chloroform, 1:9, with FeCl3: antipyrine is red, amidopyrine violet, analgin blue. For control: compare the colour reactions of the three substances and name the substances lost during re-extraction.
